turns.t: Doctor, quick, he got cleaning fluid in his eye, from the bottle, a spray!
Right, sit him here. What's your name? ~
Ravi. It burns.
Ravi, did you wash the eye out at home? ~
A bit, with the tap, a minute or two. Then we drove here. ~
How long ago did it happen?
Ten minutes. About 10 minutes.
No, it was half an hour, at least, 30 minutes, I looked at the clock when we left the house.
I'll write it down as 10 to 30 minutes. It doesn't change what I do, we're washing it out now. Do you know which cleaner it was?
Yes, I've got the bottle in my bag. It's a bathroom spray with bleach. ~
Please give it to the nurse. Ravi, can you open your eye for me? ~
It hurts. ~
I know. I'm putting numbing drops in first.
Now I'm going to wash it with lots of fluid. Look up, look down, it'll feel wet. ~
It's cold.
That's it. Keep going, we need to do this for a good ten to fifteen minutes. ~
Is he going to be blind? ~
I don't think so, but I need to examine the eye properly once it's washed. ~
Better now. ~
Good. Is your vision blurred?
A little. Not too much.
Any swelling of the eyelids?
No. Eyelids are fine.
Do you take any tablets?
He takes cetirizine, 10 mg, I think, maybe? For his asthma and hay fever.
Right. I'll note what you tell me. Pulse and oxygen for me. ~
Okay. ~
Pulse 86, oxygen 99 percent.
I've checked the surface with a dye and a blue light. There's a patch on the surface of the eye where the cells have been damaged, mostly in the lower half.
Will it heal? ~
I can't be certain yet. This could be a chemical burn of the surface, and I can't rule out deeper damage until the eye specialist has seen him.
Do we go to another hospital? ~
No, the eye team is here, and I'd like them to see him now. I'll also check the acidity of the eye, the pH, to make sure it's been washed clean.
Will I be able to go home? ~
Possibly after the specialist sees you. Don't rub the eye, and keep the bottle with the nurse.
Thank you, doctor. ~
